Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel is a notoriously difficult thinker, and students sometimes ask me how I came to be interested in his philosophy, which I have now been studying and writing about for more than three decades. In fact, it was the difficulty that attracted me, and still does. When I was studying at the Université de Paris IV Sorbonne, almost every philosophy course carried some reference to the 19th-century German idealist. If the subject was politics, the professor referred to Hegel’s notion of the state. History? The reference was to the dialectical progression of something called Spirit. Religion? Art? The mind? Hegel seemed to have something pertinent to say about all these human pursuits.

And yet, when I turned to Hegel’s texts themselves, they were almost impenetrable or, at best, enigmatic, revealing their secrets only sparingly. Nonetheless, I always had the feeling that something was going on, that something important was there to be discovered. So I persisted. As I suspected, something important is indeed going on, and even after years of study, Hegel’s thought still provides rewards and insights along with new puzzles and challenges. In both its depth and breadth, Hegel’s philosophy is perhaps rivalled only by that of Aristotle.

I am sometimes also asked to provide a brief summary of Hegel’s philosophy. This is especially challenging given its encyclopaedic reach and conceptual difficulties. Where to start? Dialectics? History? Consciousness? Spirit? The idea of systematic science? The question has forced me to come up with something more fundamental, something simple, essential and generally understandable. Indeed, I believe that every great philosopher has some basic intuition or insight that animates their reflection and underlies their enterprise, regardless of how elaborate, intricate and systematic its form may be. For Hegel, it is a belief in the agency of thought. What does that mean?

It means that you have to imagine thought coming out of your head and into the world. Thinking is an activity that is not contained in the cerebral box. It goes out into the world and works on it, participates in it, transforms it. In Hegelian terms, thought negates, determines and elevates objectivity by making it meaningful. The pen on my desk is not just a piece of blue plastic with a metal nib that I understand as a writing instrument. In fact, in apprehending it, my thought has already configured it as a writing instrument, something that I can take up in my hand and use to make notes or write a grocery list or my memoirs. As agency, thought is inherently free and active. In fact, as we’ll see, it is virtually synonymous with freedom itself.

As agency, thought also implies the existence of an agent and, for Hegel, the agent of thought is simply selfhood. Channelling René Descartes’s ‘I think, therefore I am,’ Hegel gets rid of the ‘therefore’ so it becomes ‘I think and I am.’ To be a self (an ‘I’) is to perform thinking agency in the world and that agency is an expression of the self’s essential freedom. The agency of thought is the essence of Hegel’s idealism, the belief that ideas have real purchase in reality. As such, it stands against materialism the same way that freedom stands against determinism. The question is: how does something as immaterial as thought actually take place in the material world?

Idealism is a humanism

The idealist way of thinking about thinking runs against the dominant contemporary view, in which thought is reduced to a kind of data-processing activity, following a computational model. We are fed data through our senses, which we dutifully process in our brains, which are hardwired to calculate according to certain programs, such as self-preservation, problem-solving, acquiring things, and so on. This model of thinking is largely materialist. Thought is confined to neural activity. It is also reduced to manipulating data that is supplied from outside us, on which we are dependent. Further, in reducing thought to computational calculation, we find ourselves compared with actual computers and ultimately with AI. In such comparisons, we human data-processors generally lose. The Hegelian reason for such failure is simply that computing is not what human thinking does best.

Processing and calculating is only a tiny subset of what thinking actually is and does. When we think, we create, we desire, we imagine, we will, we hope, we dread, we doubt, we suspect, we scheme, we forgive, we resent, we dream, and we also process and compute. Paradoxically, the reduction of our thinking activity to that subset is itself the result of our free thinking, by which we choose to configure the world and ourselves on a very specific, reduced horizon. In other words, conceiving the world as data and ourselves as its processors is itself an expression of our status as free thinkers. This is important because how we conceive of thought reflects on our selfhood and ultimately on our humanity. How we know says a lot about who we are.

Thinking otherness

The agency of thought liberates us from occupying the role of passive data-processors, operating on pre-established or hardwired programs. However, the question then arises as to the nature of the world that our thought acts upon – what about this world where our thought takes place? What can we say about the objectivity or reality that the freethinking agency of selfhood acts upon? If the world is open to our thought, allowing itself to be made meaningful by us, then it must be something other than the neutral sense material that feeds the data-processing model of thought. On the other hand, if the objective world is simply the product of our thinking agency, if it is there as we think it, then how is there any real objectivity? Does the world itself not simply become a feature of our thinking? This is a problem that haunts idealism. What is the status of the real world as the object of our thinking, and how can we know it as something other than ourselves? Knowing the world implies that it is something other than ourselves and yet something that is accessible to our thinking agency.

Thinking my body

The problem of how our thought relates to worldly otherness arises immediately and existentially when we make ourselves the object of our thought, when we think ourselves. How can the same entity that I am be both the subject and the object of thought? Perhaps when I think of myself as an object of my thought, then I think of my body, as distinct from my thinking agency. But then, what is the relation between my thinking and my body? If thinking agency comes out of my head and into the world, then what is the status of my head? Certainly, I cannot think of my thought as completely disembodied because then it would not be mine, would not be situated in me, and would not be seen from my point of view.

Without particular embodiment, thought would dissolve into universality and there would be no objects to think at all, since the objects of the world are always there for my body, situated in relation to it. Indeed, I could not be conscious without anything, including myself, to be conscious of. The problem becomes even more pronounced if we associate, as Hegel does, the agency of thought with freedom. Real freedom implies an objective world against which and within which my body, as the agent of my thought, can measure itself.

The Other thinks back

The problem of thinking otherness becomes crucial when the objects of our thought are other people, other selves. The agency of thought seems to imply taking others as objects, and yet, in doing so, I cannot really know them for what they are: selves with their own thinking agency, an agency that takes me or at least my body as its object. But I am not just an object for other people. I am a self! In thinking of me as their object, other people seem to deny my selfhood, my thinking agency.

The agency of thought, the idea that it takes place and has purchase outside our heads, in the physical world, delivers us onto the shores of metaphysics, and invites us to think beyond (meta) the natural world (phusis or physis). And once we are there, on those strange shores where thinking seeks to know such absolute objects as the truth of selfhood (that is, the soul) and the nature of objectivity, can thinking be restrained from attempting to grasp the Absolute itself? Once its free agency is acknowledged, thinking inevitably seeks to know the maximum of things, the Truth itself.

urn:id:9062.html: Compassion is important – not just because it makes us sensitive to the suffering of others, but because practising it can make our brains more resilient and our relationships stronger. And, as the US psychiatrist and educator Tracey Marks discusses in this video, we can actively cultivate more compassion for ourselves and for others every day. After taking a brief dive into the neuroscience of compassion, Marks talks viewers through what’s known as the ‘loving-kindness meditation’. Rooted in ancient Buddhism, this practice has been shown to have myriad benefits, including improving mood and relationships. For more on compassion, read the Psyche Idea ‘Self-compassion is not self-indulgence: here’s how to try it’ (2021).

I began climbing because I’d developed a fear of falling. A few unlucky stumbles, cartoonish in the details of how they happened – tripping over my own feet, for instance, while posing for a selfie with a burrito – were serious enough to require a dozen stitches and months of physiotherapy. I began to feel estranged from my body, as if my limbs had all developed different ideas on what to do when the ground fell away. I would work it out on the wall, I resolved, disentangle my jangling nerves while clinging to a climbing hold a few feet above the ground – a sort of exposure therapy.

What I hadn’t realised then is how well suited climbing is to ADHD brains like mine. After my first climb – a meandering route of neon pink, easy-to-grip ‘jugs’ in an indoor gym – my mind felt clearer, as if someone had cranked the volume all the way down. There was no room to think about anything other than the puzzle at hand, which took both my brain and body to solve.

Research on how climbing intersects with ADHD is limited, but online forums are filled with firsthand accounts. There’s something about the complexity of movement, the short bursts of focus it requires, and the near-instant gratification of ‘sending’ a route that might be of particular appeal to the ADHD brain. ‘It’s almost comical,’ writes one climber, ‘that a sport capable of making someone’s nervous system feel like it’s being chased by a pack of wolves … actually ends up lessening my anxiety.’ Perhaps this isn’t so surprising: the typical drug treatment for ADHD, after all, is stimulants.

My fear of falling hasn’t dissipated; as a beginner, I’m more drawn to top-rope climbing, where I’m securely attached while I dangle above the ground. But I’m glad to have… stumbled, shall we say, into an activity that lets me take a proper break from my brain.

In 1975, a collection of Mother Teresa’s thoughts and reflections was published as a short book titled A Gift for God: Prayers and Meditation. In one passage, she reflects on the best way to bring about change in the world:

If there are people who feel that God wants them to change the structures of society, that is something between them and their God. We must serve him in whatever way we are called. I am called to help the individual; to love each poor person. Not to deal with institutions. I am in no position to judge.

A simpler version of this idea would later become widely shared online as ‘If you want to change the world, go home and love your family.’

But Mother Teresa was wrong. Or at least her view of changing the world was incomplete. As a dedicated and empathetic servant to the needy, she modelled how each of us, as individuals, ought to treat each other, as individuals. But there’s more to virtue than how we think, feel, and act toward others.

In fact, it’s crucial to keep sight of what exactly Mother Teresa tells us to ignore: changing the institutions and structures of society.

‘Virtue ethics’ is the study of what good people are like. What choices do they make? What traits do they have? This way of thinking about ethics is something we all engage in – it’s not just for philosophers. It appears when Christians ask themselves ‘What would Jesus do?’ or when other seekers follow the model of Muhammad or Buddha. A casual version of it even emerges when parents encourage their kids to enjoy shows or books with positive messages about kindness or honesty.

Most forms of virtue ethics in the Western tradition, including Mother Teresa’s, share a common assumption: that being a good individual means being good to other individuals. We can find early versions of this idea expressed in Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, written more than 2,300 years ago: ‘The best man is not he who exercises his virtue towards himself but he who exercises it towards another; for this is a difficult task.’

Those who seek to change the world through justice aim to create virtuous institutions

The pursuit of this kind of interpersonal virtue can be found today across popular culture. TV shows like The Good Place (2016-20) and Ted Lasso (2020-) explore the everyday dilemmas people encounter in navigating social life: whether it’s ever OK to lie; how much we should take someone’s intentions into account when they do something wrong; when and how to forgive. Sometimes, these shows address broader social and political issues, such as wealth inequality and climate change, but when they do, the real question is still whether individual virtue is possible in an unjust world: is it irresponsible to buy fast fashion when clothes made by exploited workers are all you can afford? Are you a hypocrite for driving a gas guzzler if you care about climate change? Can you be good in a bad world?

But this long emphasis on the individual – stretching from Aristotle to Ted Lasso and beyond – hasn’t gone unquestioned. In the past, some philosophers have called instead for changing underlying laws and systems, suggesting that the quest for individual virtue is at best irrelevant and at worst counterproductive. This creates a division between those seeking justice and those seeking virtue. Those who seek to change the world through justice aim to create virtuous institutions. In the process, however, they sometimes take human vices for granted.

Consider Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who begins his political treatise The Social Contract (1762) by proposing that individuals should be taken ‘as they are’ while laws should be taken ‘as they might be’. Like Plato and Thomas Hobbes before him (and John Stuart Mill and Philippa Foot after), he thought that the way to make the world more just is to design well-functioning laws and institutions. These function well, supposedly, when they’re based on an accurate understanding of human psychology. We need laws – by which Rousseau means a whole political system – that suit the kinds of creatures we are.

This approach is the opposite of Mother Teresa’s, who in effect took laws as they are, and individuals as they might be.

But there are more than two ways to change the world. Focusing on virtue to the exclusion of justice is insufficient. So is focusing on justice to the exclusion of virtue.

For the past few years, along with the philosopher Daniel Kelly, we’ve been considering a third way. This is the result of research into what we call ‘structure-facing virtues’.

These virtues are skills and traits of character that can help individuals create larger change through the transformation of social systems. They’re individual in the sense that they are skills anyone can learn. They’re also structural in the sense that their target is institutions and laws.

Being antiracist means working affirmatively against the social structures driving racial injustice

For example, what comes to mind when you’re asked to imagine how a good person would live in a world rife with racial injustice? For many people, it would likely involve treating everyone with dignity and respect, or treating others based on the content of their character rather than the colour of their skin. It would focus on avoiding being racist.

But not being racist is just a way of being kinder to the people you come in contact with. It doesn’t address the big forces that allow racism to create widespread suffering. A better option is being antiracist, which means working affirmatively against the social structures driving racial injustice. This entails working to change power relations, laws and unjust social systems, from the housing regulations that reinforce segregation to the educational inequities that shape people’s opportunities.

Antiracism is one of many structure-facing virtues. Below, we present four key features to help you understand what other forms might look like. Despite what Mother Teresa says, these are how you change the world.

When something goes wrong, how do we explain it? Typically, we look for someone to blame. If a co-worker arrives late to the office and delays a meeting, your first thought might be that they’re lazy and weren’t disciplined enough to get ready on time. That would be an ‘individualistic’ explanation. Another explanation is that they may have left early but got stuck in unforeseeable traffic. That would be a ‘situational’ explanation. Or maybe they got stuck in traffic because they have to drive farther than other employees, and they have to drive farther because that’s where the affordable homes are. That would be a ‘structural’ explanation.

Research demonstrates that individuals can, through targeted practice, learn to avoid individualistic explanations. But it’s not enough to simply consider how external factors might affect outcomes. We’ve got to know which external factors matter, and how. Structure-facing virtues require genuine understanding.

Some children are assuming these inequalities are fair because individuals are getting what they deserve

The second feature is understanding. Developmental psychology has put the gap between seeing and understanding social structures on full display. Consider research showing that young children infer social status from the regularities they observe. In India, children as young as five say that Indian-English speakers are ‘worse leaders’ than British-English speakers. In the US, children as young as seven will tell you that women have lower-status jobs than men, and that Black people have less money than white people.

Children are seeing these differences in social status, but not necessarily understanding them. Some of them default to meritocratic (individualistic) explanations for what they observe. They are assuming that these inequalities are fair because individuals are getting what they deserve.

But other children – especially if their parents talk openly with them about status and unfairness – come to question these social structures. They’re on the road to understanding them.

Still, it’s one thing to understand how social structures go wrong. It’s another to believe they can be altered. Structure-facing virtues require us to see structures as changeable. This is the third feature.

Popular thinking about changeability has been shaped by the American psychologist Carol Dweck, who introduced the contrast between ‘growth mindsets’ and ‘fixed mindsets’. Having a growth mindset means emphasising the power of development through practice and de-emphasising the limits posed by innate, fixed talent. As coaches around the world tell their players: just try to get a little better every day.

Growth mindsets are often invoked to improve individuals’ academic (or athletic) trajectories, but their effectiveness has been questioned. Some high-profile attempts to replicate growth mindset interventions have failed. Large studies have found small average effects. Relatedly, critics have challenged growth mindset research for being too individualistic. Perhaps the idea that kids can succeed if they adopt the right mindset about themselves is another misbegotten way to put all the responsibility on them for their success, ignoring structural obstacles such as poverty and educational inequities.

Those who believe that institutions can change even a little bit are more likely to fight to change them

These concerns have some merit, but they miss the mark in two ways. First, follow-up studies consistently find that teachers’ mindsets matter, too. If teachers just hang up growth mindset posters in their classrooms or passionlessly recite talking points about intelligence being like a muscle, kids tune out the message. But if teachers themselves believe their students can grow and improve, and then organise their classes around that outcome, children will take the opportunity to prove their teachers right. People need the right environment to grow – the right social structures and role models. Properly understood, research on growth mindsets vindicates the importance of seeing and understanding structures rather than drawing our attention away from them.

What about the criticism that mindset research is too individualistic? It’s true that most people are focused on improving the students themselves. The typical assumption is that growth mindsets help kids climb the existing socioeconomic ladder. But what about tearing down that ladder? Here, too, a broader look at the research paints a richer picture: people can learn to adopt growth mindsets toward social systems. Those who believe that institutions can change even a little bit are more likely to fight to change them. And, in fighting, they prove themselves right.

Seeing structures, understanding them, and knowing they’re changeable isn’t worth much if we don’t take action. What leads people to take the next step, and act to challenge the status quo?

Some answers are familiar. People are more likely to take action when they’re outraged by its unfairness, and when it’s outrageously unfair to them. But some precursors to taking action are more surprising.

Changemakers know they can make a difference to each other. They show up for their friends, neighbours and family

One important element is a person’s comfort with uncertainty; people who get involved in fights for justice tend to be more comfortable than others in recognising that they don’t know what the future holds.

Perhaps even more surprising is the attitude the most engaged changemakers have toward their own power to make a difference. Changemakers the world over, from participants in the 1964 Mississippi Freedom Summer to the organisers behind the Arab Spring, don’t typically have grandiose expectations about their own unique power to effect change. They don’t assume the fight will be lost unless they, personally, turn up.

Rather, people who challenge the status quo know they can make a difference to each other. They show up for their friends, neighbours and family. They show up for the people whose fate they recognise is closely linked to their own. Here we see where structure-facing virtue really acts as a ‘third way’ – between individuals and institutions.

Virtue ethics is indeed valuable for learning how to live well together. But being a good person is not only related to the way we treat the person standing right in front of us. It bears on how we make the social world, too, and how we work together to change it when it needs fixing.

Have you ever been so completely absorbed in what you were doing that nothing else seemed to matter? Where your total focus on your task or activity led you to perform effortlessly, without self-consciousness?

These moments of complete absorption – when you’re so immersed in what you’re doing that everything else (including your ‘inner critic’) falls away – are among the most rewarding experiences we can have. Psychologists call it ‘flow’, and it is more accessible than you might realise. In this Guide, I’m going to share with you some practical strategies for experiencing more flow in your life.

The idea of flow as a universal human experience was put forward by the Hungarian American psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. As a researcher of intrinsic motivation, Csikszentmihalyi had studied artists to understand how they spent hours, days and weeks on developing their paintings, only to put them aside once finished and move on to the next one. After this initial study, Csikszentmihalyi turned to people engaged in diverse activities – from basketball to chess, from dancing to surgery – and found they described their experiences of total task-engagement in very similar ways, often using the word ‘flow’.

Flow is an optimal state of consciousness. In flow, we feel at one with the activity. In flow terms, this is known as action-awareness merging. For an actor, there ceases to be a separation between the character being played and the self. For a musician, this oneness can be experienced as a sense that the instrument being played is an extension of their body.

This sense of action and awareness merging comes about from the total focus we bring to the activity. Total concentration on the task at hand is probably the clearest sign of being in flow, and is often what lifts the quality of performance to the next level.

When in flow, we have a sense of control over our actions and lose any fear of failure that might otherwise be present when engaging in an important performance. We also let go of any concern for how others may be perceiving us. This loss of self-consciousness is one of the most liberating aspects of flow. For example, in giving a presentation, we let go of thoughts about how well we are doing, and what the audience may be thinking of us up on stage, and instead we become absorbed by the task in front of us – a sure-fire way to let go of the common fear of public speaking.

Sometimes, during a flow experience, we lose track of time. Reading an enthralling book, you may finally put it down and be surprised that hours have passed. The way time passes in flow is perceptibly different to the actual passage of time. Sometimes, a captivating hour-long event seems to be over in a matter of minutes. At other times, such as when performing complex movements in a small space of time, you might feel that you have all the time in the world to complete the action. Standing at bat to a fast-pitch softball, as we take swing, we are so attuned to the ball that we can see the seams on it as it rotates straight towards the sweet spot on our bat.

Flow is highly rewarding and motivates us to keep engaging in an activity. This characteristic of flow is known as an autotelic, or self-rewarding, experience. Over time, if you can find flow in your work, hobby or creative endeavours, you will create for yourself a rich and meaningful life. And, ultimately, it is the quality of experience we have as we go through life that matters, as so eloquently put by Csikszentmihalyi in his paper ‘Toward a Psychology of Optimal Experience’ (1982): ‘It is useful to remember occasionally that life unfolds as a chain of subjective experiences … The quality of these experiences determines whether and to what extent life was worth living.’

Your mission: to infiltrate an organisation of animal rights activists. You must arrive at the office with a smile on your face. You must wear wool-free jackets, silk-free ties, and leather-free belts. You must pretend that they are all haute couture. You must consume only cheeseless pizzas.

Do you hear me? No cheese, ever.

You may encounter obstacles during your mission. You may accidentally wear a 95 per cent polyester and 5 per cent wool cardigan one day. On that day, a coworker will see your cardigan from across the room and, via a yet-unstudied form of evolved vegan ganglia, sense its violent woollen contents. She will abandon her work and lope across the room to compliment it. She will peer into your eyes, stroke your cardigan with studied awe and ask: ‘Does this have wool in it?’ You must not crumple beneath her morally superior gaze. In fact, on this day, your coworker’s aggression is simply a power play. She wants your job and hopes to get you fired by loudly insinuating in front of your boss that you own a wool cardigan.

Who am I, to give you such a mission? Well, I am you, talking to you from the other side.

It is 2013. You are a drunk who, despite a promising high-school career and two Ivy League degrees, buckled under the force of your self-destruction and moved back to the state where you grew up. To make matters worse, you are a writer. You take on side hustles and thankless gigs in pursuit of literary greatness; you wonder if your landlord will accept Beanie Babies as rent. You can change your career path if you want; it’s early enough. But that would be giving up. Also, a nearby animal rights organisation has a content writing job available. It’s the only writing job in the entire region. So, here you are.

In your public-facing role, you’ll be required to become vegan. But that will be the easy part. For three months, you’ll even enjoy it. You’ll consume less fat and wake up energised. You’ll drip sriracha sauce on seitan strips and announce that you’re Gordon Ramsay. You’ll lose weight, sure, and you’ll feel weak on the days you forget to consume nutritional yeast, but you’ll feel more centred. You’ll even stop drinking. You will enjoy channelling all your displaced anger into a hatred for milk.

It’s everything else that will make your life hell. At every party you’re invited to, people will ask you where you work and you’ll have to tell them. Many people hate vegans with a passion so profound that scientists have devoted whole careers to studying it, and those at your organisation are apparently to blame. Your career move will make you the de facto wet blanket of every social gathering, straining all your friendships, and you’ll be forced to befriend – are you prepared for this? – your coworkers.

One of those coworkers will report you to your superiors for ordering an after-work cocktail while wearing a shirt with your organisation’s logo on it. Strangely, she won’t explain that this is against company policy until after you tell her you’re buying drinks, ask what she wants, and buy her a Coke. Another, whom you’ll invite to your house for a party because she seems more laid back than the others, will accuse you of ‘forcing violence’ on your cat after you ambush him with his favourite stuffed animal and play-fight with him for 15 seconds. At work, your boss, who prides himself on a glitteringly dark sense of humour, will laugh when a ceiling collapses onto a PTA meeting at a high-school auditorium: ‘They were probably all non-vegan,’ he’ll say, as you force out a titter.

You’ll drunkenly pop shrimp into your mouth; a young woman nearby will record a video of you

You’ll begin to understand why people hate vegans more than they hate veganism.

Don’t give up. Rent is due soon. You can rendezvous with your compatriots, the non-animal-activists, outside of work hours. Meet in vegan-free localities where your coworkers won’t find you or hear you use local expressions such as ‘kill two birds with one stone’. Think Ruth’s Chris Steak House. But then you’ll meet your compatriots at a New Year’s Eve party that you stupidly told your coworkers about. You’ll relapse and drunkenly pop shrimp into your mouth; a young woman at the adjoining table will record a video of you. You’ll recognise her face for a moment. You’ve seen her at the building.

You’re just being paranoid, you’ll tell yourself.

Suddenly, your boss will begin to act cold towards you. He’ll adjust your job description and assign you more administrative work. The writing aspect of your job, the reason you stayed so long, is slipping through your fingers. You will break at this point. You’ll sneak away during your lunch hour and buy a Grilled Stuft Burrito from Taco Bell, your first in a long time. Trembling, you’ll recline your car seat in the restaurant’s parking lot and huddle down to eat it as sweat beads on your forehead – a wary, hunted animal, guilty for having reverted to your true self. You’ll Febreze yourself to mask the scent of chicken, and then return to work flashing a shiitake-eating grin.

Soon, you’ll become bold enough to start visiting Wendy’s, a most decidedly non-vegan-friendly restaurant. One afternoon you’ll forget to Febreze yourself, earning yourself a lunchtime tail the next day. Trundling through the drive-thru, you’ll shake your head; no way is that Autumn from Accounting, frowning at you through your rear-view mirror. The next day, your co-worker, the one who accused you of training your cat to become a warlord, will invite you on an after-work stroll.

‘Have you had any Frostys lately?’ she’ll ask, and you’ll realise the jig is up.

You can do one of two things when this happens. You can quit your job and abandon the mission with your dignity intact, or you can wait to get yourself fired. You will choose the latter.

So one day, you’ll bring in a salad containing goat cheese and eat it at your desk, allowing its potent, animal-murdering smell to pervade the Campaigns Department. At first, you’ll hear your boss emit a clipped, nettled cough. Then the furious typing will begin: your coworkers are messaging about your lunch decision. The room will erupt into teary-eyed, performative coughing, and several people will evacuate the office as if they’re running from a car bomb. You will finish your salad in peace.

Alas, the strength of your writing will be enough that you keep your job.

Stop for a moment. Why are you doing this? You still need the money. And this is not your first difficult assignment, is it? When you were 12, you recognised that you were inattentive and impulsive, and chose to mask those symptoms from the world because neurodivergence didn’t exist yet. For the subsequent decade, you barred your inner life from peers, mentors and family, accumulating internal pressure, cultivating an anxiety disorder, practising your smile. You lived a double life for 10 years. Is that why you want to blow it all up now?

The pleather shoe drops: your direct supervisor tells you to order no further banners

In the end, you target the boss himself. You know exactly what to do. You’ve seen him turn his departmental reports into standup routines at televised company meetings; you know that he loves being the centre of attention. When it’s finally your turn to represent your department at the meeting, you decide to one-up him. You draw upon your full powers as a comedian and invoke the humour of Kathy Griffin, spinning an update about the Pamela Anderson Foundation into an anecdote about buying socks from a drag queen. Some jokes fall flat but most land; you have the audience in the palm of your KFC-crumb-covered hand. You are the captain now. At the back of the auditorium, your glowering boss skulks from the room.

You go back to your desk and order more sky banners attacking SeaWorld. Then the pleather shoe drops: your direct supervisor tells you to order no further banners. You are fired for being ‘five minutes late’ that day.

Relief fills your body. Relief, triumph, and… something else. You realise: you could have spent that time looking for another job. You just took out a car loan. You have no other source of income. You barely have any savings. You relapsed at a New Year’s Eve party. You have isolated yourself from all your friends from college and journalism school. You have high cholesterol from eating so many Wendy’s hamburgers.

Shock. You feel shock.

Are you prepared for all of that? Or do you want to fast-forward to 2026, when you’re eight years sober and no longer hitting the self-destruct button every time you’re cornered?

It’s not a bad feeling. I’m still broke, but I write about things that interest me. I manage my anxiety and ADHD. I tackle problems with grace. I let people in.

I really wish you could fast-forward. But this is your mission, and the only way out is through.

urn:id:9036.html: Timothy Gant Jr (aka Teddy) is one of just a handful of male birth doulas in the state of Texas. In her short documentary Teddy, the US director Lauren Santucci profiles Gant, exploring how the circumstances of his own birth, the high maternal mortality rate among Black women in the United States and his identity as a ‘natural protector’ led him to his unusual calling. In her affecting portrait, Santucci captures Gant at his day job as a security guard, in conversation with his mother and guiding a young Black couple through their first childbirth with knowledge, calm and care. Through Gant’s story, the film challenges and reframes conventions around the meaning of masculinity.
